title: Punctuation That Changes the Meaning
bigQuestion: How can a mark smaller than a letter change who gets the money, who said what, and what a sentence means?

story.title: The Comma Worth a House
story.kicker: Picture a will with one sentence in it, and two family members who read that sentence two different ways.
paragraphs: Imagine an old woman in a small Illinois town who writes her own will at her kitchen table because a lawyer seems like a waste of money. She has a brother named Walter and a sister named June, and she is fond of both. She writes one sentence: I leave everything I own to my brother, and my sister. She signs it, folds it, and puts it in a drawer. Years later she dies, and the sentence goes to a probate court, the court that sorts out what a will means.

Walter's lawyer reads the sentence one way. The gift, he says, is to my brother. Then comes a comma, and the words and my sister are a stray afterthought, tacked on, not part of the gift. Perhaps she meant to add June and never finished the thought. June's lawyer reads it the other way. Everything goes to my brother and my sister together, he argues, and the comma is just a pause the old woman heard in her head. Two readers, one comma, and a house, a car and a savings account hanging on it.

This story is invented, but the argument is not. Courts really do spend days on commas, because a legal document has no author standing beside it to explain what she meant. The sentence must carry its whole meaning on its own. A single comma before and in a pair, where none is needed, opened a gap that two smart people could drive their arguments through. Had she written to my brother and my sister, equally, there would have been no case.

Nobody expects you to write a will this year. But every text, essay, caption and email you send goes out into the world without you standing next to it. A semicolon, a dash, a pair of commas around a clause, a hyphen between two words: each one tells your reader how the parts of your sentence fit together. This chapter is about those marks, what each one promises, and how a small one can change who gets the house.
story.think: The old woman knew exactly what she meant. Why was that not enough? Where in your own writing does a reader have only your words and nothing else?

lessons.title: The Semicolon
lessons.mainIdea: A semicolon joins two complete sentences that belong together, and it separates items in a list whose items already contain commas.
reading: Read these two versions. The storm knocked out the power. We ate dinner by candlelight. Now: The storm knocked out the power; we ate dinner by candlelight. The period says these are two separate facts. The *semicolon* says they are two halves of one thought, the second following from the first. A semicolon can join two independent clauses only, two groups of words that could each stand alone as a sentence. That is the whole test. If either side could not be a sentence on its own, the semicolon is wrong.

The semicolon is stronger than a comma and weaker than a period. Writers use it when the ideas are so close that a period would feel like slamming a door. It also fixes a comma splice without adding a word: The bus was late, I missed the quiz becomes The bus was late; I missed the quiz. When the second clause begins with a connecting word like however, therefore, meanwhile or for example, the semicolon goes before that word and a comma after it: The bus was late; however, the teacher let me take the quiz after school. A comma alone before however is a splice.

The semicolon has a second job that has nothing to do with clauses. In a list where the items themselves contain commas, use semicolons to separate the items, so the reader can see where each one ends: The trip stops in Springfield, Illinois; St. Louis, Missouri; and Memphis, Tennessee. Without the semicolons that list looks like six places. One caution: a semicolon is not a fancy colon. It does not introduce a list or an explanation. Use it to join equals or to organize a crowded list, and nowhere else.

words.d: the mark ; that joins two independent clauses or separates list items that contain commas
a group of words with a subject and verb that could stand alone as a sentence
two independent clauses joined by only a comma, which is an error

look.title: Slam or Lean
look.text: Version 1: She did not call. I did not expect her to. Version 2: She did not call; I did not expect her to. Version 3: She did not call, and I did not expect her to. All three are correct. Read each one aloud and listen to the pause between the two halves.
look.prompt: Which version sounds most bitter, which sounds most tired, and which sounds most matter-of-fact? What does the punctuation have to do with the tone?

check.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: The rain stopped; the streets began to dry.
The rain stopped; and the streets began to dry.
After the rain stopped; the streets began to dry.
The rain stopped; drying the streets.
check.why: Both halves are independent clauses. The others put a semicolon before a joining word, after a dependent clause, or before a phrase.

check.q: 'I studied all night, however, I still felt unprepared.' How should this be punctuated?
choices: Leave it as it is
I studied all night; however, I still felt unprepared.
I studied all night, however; I still felt unprepared.
I studied all night however I still felt unprepared.
check.why: However starts a second independent clause, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

check.q: When should semicolons separate items in a list?
choices: When the list has more than five items
When the list comes after a colon
When the items themselves contain commas
Whenever the list contains place names
check.why: Semicolons make the boundaries between items clear when commas are already in use inside the items.

lessons.title: The Colon
lessons.mainIdea: A colon follows a complete sentence and announces what comes next: a list, an explanation or a quotation.
reading: A *colon* is a pointer. It says: here it comes. She packed three things: a flashlight, a map and a sandwich. The words before the colon make a complete sentence, She packed three things, and the words after it deliver what that sentence promised. That is the one rule most writers get wrong. The part before the colon must be able to stand alone. She packed: a flashlight, a map and a sandwich is incorrect, because She packed is not a finished thought. If you would not put a period there, do not put a colon there either.

A colon can introduce a list, but it can also introduce a single word or a whole explanation. There was only one thing she wanted: sleep. The plan failed for a simple reason: nobody had checked the weather. In the second sentence, the words after the colon are a full clause that explains the words before it. This is where a colon does something a semicolon cannot. A semicolon joins two equals; a colon makes the second part answer the first. Read the sentence and ask whether the second half explains, lists or names what the first half set up. If yes, the colon fits.

Colons also introduce a longer quotation in an essay, after a complete sentence: Douglass describes the moment plainly: and then the quotation follows. And they have small mechanical jobs: between hours and minutes (7:45), after the greeting in a formal letter (Dear Dr. Ortiz:), and between a title and subtitle. Whether to capitalize the first word after a colon is a matter of style; the usual rule is to capitalize only if what follows is a complete sentence and your style guide asks for it. MLA does not require it. Pick one practice and keep to it.

words.d: the mark : that follows a complete sentence and introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation
a second, explaining title that follows the main title after a colon
a published set of rules for punctuation, format and citation, such as MLA

look.title: Would You Put a Period There?
look.text: Sentence A: The recipe needs: eggs, flour and milk. Sentence B: The recipe needs three things: eggs, flour and milk. Sentence C: The recipe is simple: eggs, flour and milk. Cover everything after the colon in each one and read what is left.
look.prompt: Which sentences pass the period test, and which fails? Rewrite the failing one two ways: once by removing the colon and once by fixing the words before it.

check.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
choices: The team needs: a coach, a field and uniforms.
The team needs a coach: and a field and uniforms.
The team needs, a coach: a field and uniforms.
The team needs three things: a coach, a field and uniforms.
check.why: The words before the colon form a complete sentence, and the list after it delivers what they promise.

check.q: What can a colon do that a semicolon cannot?
choices: Make the second part explain or deliver what the first part set up
Join two independent clauses
Separate items in a complicated list
End a sentence
check.why: A semicolon joins equals; a colon points forward so the second part answers the first.

check.q: Why is 'My favorite foods are: pizza and tacos' incorrect?
choices: Because a colon cannot introduce only two items
Because the words before the colon are not a complete sentence
Because pizza should be capitalized
Because a semicolon is required
check.why: My favorite foods are is unfinished, so the colon interrupts the sentence instead of following it.

lessons.title: Dashes and Parentheses
lessons.mainIdea: A dash breaks a sentence for emphasis or a sudden turn; parentheses tuck in a quiet aside.
reading: There are two kinds of dash and one hyphen, and they look almost alike. The hyphen is short and joins words (well-known). The *em dash* is long, about the width of the letter m, and it breaks a sentence: She opened the box and found the one thing she had not expected, a letter from her father. Replace that comma with an em dash and the letter arrives with a jolt. A dash creates a pause with drama in it. One dash sets off something at the end of a sentence. Two dashes set off something in the middle, like a louder pair of commas: The dog, a huge, muddy, joyful animal, knocked over the lamp.

Because dashes shout, they lose their power if you use them everywhere. A page with a dash in every sentence sounds breathless. Use one where a comma feels too soft and a colon feels too formal: a sharp turn, a surprise, a summing up. Parentheses do the opposite job. They lower the voice. The meeting (which nobody wanted) ran two hours. The words inside the parentheses are an aside the reader could skip. If the aside matters, use dashes or commas instead. Punctuation belonging to the main sentence goes outside the closing parenthesis, unless the whole sentence is inside.

The shorter *en dash*, about the width of an n, shows a range: pages 12–15, the 2024–25 season, the Chicago–Milwaukee train. Many people type a hyphen there and no reader minds. On a phone or a keyboard the em dash is often typed as two hyphens, and most word processors convert them. The more important skill is choosing. Commas, dashes and parentheses can all set off the same words; which one you pick tells the reader how much to care. Commas are neutral, dashes point, parentheses whisper.

words.d: a long dash that breaks a sentence for emphasis, a turn or an interruption
a medium dash that shows a range, such as pages 12–15
the curved marks ( ) that set off a quiet aside the reader could skip
a remark added to a sentence that is not part of its main point

look.title: A Poet Who Loved the Dash
look.text: Hope is the thing with feathers - / That perches in the soul - / And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all -
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, poem beginning Hope is the thing with feathers, written about 1861 (dashes printed as hyphens here)
look.prompt: Dickinson used dashes where most writers would use commas or periods. Read the lines aloud with commas instead. What changes in the pace and the feeling?

check.q: What is the difference between a dash and parentheses, in the lesson's terms?
choices: A dash is for quotations; parentheses are for numbers
A dash goes only at the end of a sentence
Dashes point and add emphasis; parentheses whisper an aside
Parentheses are longer than dashes
check.why: Both can set off the same words, but a dash raises the volume while parentheses lower it.

check.q: Which mark shows a range of pages or years?
choices: The hyphen
The em dash
The semicolon
The en dash
check.why: The en dash shows ranges such as pages 12–15 or the 2024–25 season.

check.q: Why does the lesson warn against using dashes in every sentence?
choices: Because a mark used everywhere stops standing out
Because dashes are never correct in formal writing
Because dashes must always come in pairs
Because dashes cannot replace commas
check.why: A dash works by contrast. Overuse makes writing breathless and takes away the effect.

lessons.title: Commas That Change the Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: A pair of commas around a clause says the clause is extra; no commas say the clause is needed to identify the noun.
reading: Read these two sentences. My brother who lives in Peoria is a nurse. My brother, who lives in Peoria, is a nurse. In the first sentence, I have more than one brother, and who lives in Peoria tells you which one I mean. In the second, I have one brother, and the clause between the commas is extra information about him. Two commas, and the size of my family changed. A clause that identifies which one is called *restrictive*: it restricts, or narrows, the noun, and it takes no commas. A clause that adds information about a noun already identified is *nonrestrictive*, and it is set off by commas.

Here is the test. Cover the clause and read the sentence without it. If the sentence still points to the same person or thing, the clause was extra: use commas. If the sentence now points to the wrong person, or to no one in particular, the clause was needed: no commas. Students who cheat will fail. Cover the clause: Students will fail. That is not what the writer meant, so the clause is restrictive. Chicago, which sits on Lake Michigan, is cold in January. Cover the clause: Chicago is cold in January. Still the same city, so the clause is nonrestrictive and the commas are right.

American editors mostly follow one more habit: that introduces restrictive clauses and which, with commas, introduces nonrestrictive ones. The car that hit the pole was red (the one that hit the pole, as opposed to others). The car, which hit the pole, was red (one car; the crash is extra). Not everyone keeps this rule, and British writers often use which for both, so a reader will forgive a slip. But the commas are not optional. They change what the sentence claims. The same logic applies to appositives, nouns that rename other nouns: My friend Luis (I have several friends) versus My best friend, Luis, (I have one best friend).

words.d: describing a clause or phrase that identifies which one is meant; it takes no commas
describing a clause or phrase that adds extra information about a noun already identified; set off by commas
a noun or noun phrase that renames the noun beside it, such as Luis in my friend Luis

look.title: How Many Sisters?
look.text: Sentence 1: Her sister who works nights never comes to dinner. Sentence 2: Her sister, who works nights, never comes to dinner. Sentence 3: The teachers who stayed late got pizza. Sentence 4: The teachers, who stayed late, got pizza.
look.prompt: For each pair, say how many sisters she has and how many teachers got pizza. Which version would a teacher who left early want the principal to have written?

check.q: 'The students who finished early may leave.' What does the lack of commas tell you?
choices: Every student finished early
Only the students who finished early may leave
The clause is extra information
The sentence is incorrect
check.why: Without commas the clause is restrictive: it narrows students to the ones who finished early.

check.q: Which sentence says the writer has only one aunt?
choices: My aunt who lives in Joliet sends cards.
My aunt that lives in Joliet sends cards.
My aunt, who lives in Joliet, sends cards.
My aunt in Joliet sends cards.
check.why: The commas make the clause nonrestrictive, extra information about the one aunt.

check.q: What is the test for whether a clause needs commas?
choices: Count the words in the clause
Check whether the clause starts with who
Move the clause to the end of the sentence
Cover the clause and see whether the sentence still points to the same thing
check.why: If the sentence still identifies the same noun without the clause, the clause is extra and takes commas.

lessons.title: Other Commas That Matter
lessons.mainIdea: Commas mark direct address, separate list items, and set off introductions, and skipping one can change who or what a sentence means.
reading: Let's eat Grandma. Let's eat, Grandma. The comma of *direct address* separates the person being spoken to from the rest of the sentence, and without it Grandma becomes dinner. The joke is old because the rule matters. Any time a sentence speaks to someone by name or title, put a comma on either side of the name: I know, Coach, that we lost. The same comma appears after yes and no (Yes, I finished) and around small interruptions (The answer, of course, is no).

In a list of three or more, commas separate the items: eggs, flour and milk. Whether to put a comma before the and is the most argued point in American punctuation. That final comma is called the *serial comma* (or Oxford comma). Newspapers usually skip it; books and MLA usually use it. Both are correct, but there are sentences where leaving it out creates a mix-up: I thanked my parents, Beyonce and the mayor reads as if my parents are Beyonce and the mayor. With the serial comma, I thanked my parents, Beyonce, and the mayor, there are four people. Pick one practice, stay consistent, and add the comma whenever it prevents confusion.

A comma follows an introductory phrase or clause: After the game, we ate. Because the bus was late, I missed the quiz. It is often skipped after a very short opener (Then we ate), but never skip it if the sentence could be misread: Before eating, the dog needs a walk versus Before eating the dog, needs a walk. Use a comma between two independent clauses joined by and, but, or, so, yet: The rain stopped, and we went outside. Do not use one when and joins only two verbs with one subject: The rain stopped and gave way to sun. Commas are not breaths. They are signals about structure, and a reader follows them.

words.d: speaking to someone by name inside a sentence; the name is set off with commas
the comma before and or or in a list of three or more, also called the Oxford comma
words that open a sentence before the main clause, usually followed by a comma

look.title: A Dedication Written for This Lesson
look.text: This book is dedicated to my teachers, Mr. Okafor and Ms. Reyes. This book is dedicated to my teachers, Mr. Okafor, and Ms. Reyes.
look.prompt: How many people are thanked in the first sentence, and how many in the second? Which sentence would you write if Mr. Okafor and Ms. Reyes were never your teachers?

check.q: What is the difference between 'Stop Marcus' and 'Stop, Marcus'?
choices: The first tells someone to stop Marcus; the second tells Marcus to stop
There is no difference
The first is a question
The second tells someone to stop Marcus
check.why: The comma of direct address shows that Marcus is being spoken to, not acted on.

check.q: When does the lesson say you should always use the serial comma?
choices: Only in newspapers
When leaving it out would cause a mix-up
Only in lists of exactly three
Never; it is always wrong
check.why: Both practices are accepted, but the comma must appear whenever its absence makes items run together.

check.q: Which sentence needs a comma?
choices: The rain stopped and gave way to sun.
We ate and then we slept.
The rain stopped and we went outside.
She ran and jumped.
check.why: The rain stopped and we went outside joins two independent clauses with and, so a comma goes before and. The others have one subject with two verbs or are very short.

lessons.title: Hyphens
lessons.mainIdea: A hyphen joins words that work together as one unit, especially two-word descriptions placed before a noun.
reading: A small dog trainer and a small-dog trainer are different people. The first is a trainer who is small; the second trains small dogs. The *hyphen* glues small to dog so the reader knows they form one description. This is the hyphen's main job: joining a *compound modifier*, two or more words that together describe the noun that follows. A well-known author. A five-year-old cousin. A last-minute change. Take away the hyphen and the reader has to guess how the words group.

The hyphen appears when the compound comes before the noun and usually disappears when it comes after. A well-known author, but the author is well known. A part-time job, but she works part time. One exception: do not hyphenate after an -ly adverb, because the -ly already shows the words belong together: a highly rated show, a badly written note. Hyphens also join numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine, fractions used as adjectives (a two-thirds majority), and some prefixes, especially before a capital letter or a repeated vowel: pre-Civil War, anti-inflammatory, re-enter.

Some compounds are always written as one word (notebook, everyday as an adjective), some as two (ice cream), and some with a hyphen (mother-in-law). These change over time; e-mail became email within a couple of decades. When you are unsure, check a current dictionary, which is what editors do. But the compound modifier rule you can apply on your own. Ask: do these words describe the noun together, as one idea? If yes, and they come before the noun, join them. A little-used road is one few people drive on; a little used road is a small road that has been used.

words.d: the short mark - that joins words into a single unit, such as well-known
two or more words that together describe the noun that follows them
a word part added to the front of a word, such as pre-, anti- or re-

look.title: Who Is Being Described?
look.text: Sign 1: Man eating shark seen near pier. Sign 2: Man-eating shark seen near pier. Sign 3: Twenty four-hour shifts. Sign 4: Twenty-four hour shifts. Each pair uses the same words in the same order.
look.prompt: Say what each sign means. In Sign 3 and Sign 4, how many shifts are there and how long is each one? What does the hyphen tell the reader in each case?

check.q: Which phrase is hyphenated correctly?
choices: a highly-rated movie
a movie that was well-made
a movie that is high quality
a well-made movie
check.why: Well-made is a compound modifier before the noun. No hyphen after an -ly adverb, and usually none after the noun.

check.q: What does the hyphen in 'small-dog trainer' tell the reader?
choices: That small and dog together describe the trainer's specialty
That the trainer is small
That the trainer works with one dog
That the phrase is a proper name
check.why: The hyphen groups small with dog as one description: a trainer of small dogs.

check.q: What should you do when unsure whether a compound is one word, two words or hyphenated?
choices: Always hyphenate to be safe
Check a current dictionary
Always write it as one word
Avoid the word entirely
check.why: Compounds change over time, so editors check a current dictionary.

lessons.title: Punctuating Dialogue
lessons.mainIdea: Quotation marks hold exactly what a speaker said, and commas, periods and speaker tags follow a fixed set of rules.
reading: Here is a line of dialogue done right: "I am not going back in there," Lena said, "until someone finds the snake." Three rules are working. First, the quotation marks surround only the spoken words. Second, the *speaker tag*, Lena said, is attached with a comma, not a period. The tag and the speech form one sentence. Third, when the tag interrupts a single sentence of speech, the second half opens with a lowercase letter, since it continues the sentence that began before the tag.

In American style, commas and periods go inside the closing quotation mark, always, even when it looks odd: She called it "a disaster." Question marks and exclamation points go inside if they belong to the quoted words and outside if they belong to the whole sentence. "Are you serious?" he asked. Did she really say "never"? When the quoted words are a question, no extra comma is added: "Where is it?" she asked, not "Where is it?," she asked.

Start a new paragraph each time the speaker changes, even if the line is one word. That paragraph break is itself punctuation. It tells the reader a different voice is speaking. A writer can sometimes drop the speaker tags and let the back-and-forth carry itself. Do not put quotation marks around indirect speech, which reports what someone said without the exact words: Lena said she was not going back in. No marks, no comma, and the pronoun shifts from I to she. Notice, too, that said is nearly invisible to readers; it does not need replacing with exclaimed or uttered every time.

words.d: the spoken words of characters, shown with quotation marks
the words that identify who is speaking, such as Lena said
reporting what someone said without their exact words, so no quotation marks are used

look.title: An Exchange Written for This Lesson
look.text:
"You took the last one," Theo said.
"I took the one nobody wanted," Ana said. "There is a difference."
"Is there?"
"Ask anyone."
look.prompt: Find every comma, period and question mark and say why it sits inside or outside the quotation marks. Why can the last two lines get away with no speaker tags?

check.q: Which line is punctuated correctly?
choices: "We won". she said.
"We won," She said.
"We won," she said.
"We won", she said.
check.why: The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark and the speaker tag begins with a lowercase letter.

check.q: Where does the question mark go in the sentence: Did the coach really say "practice is canceled"
choices: Inside the quotation marks, after canceled
After coach
Before the opening quotation mark
Outside the closing quotation mark
check.why: The whole sentence is the question, not the quoted words, so the mark goes outside.

check.q: How should indirect speech be written?
choices: Without quotation marks: Lena said she was not going back in.
With quotation marks: Lena said "she was not going back in."
With a colon: Lena said: she was not going back in.
With single quotation marks: Lena said 'she was not going back in.'
check.why: Indirect speech reports the words without quoting them exactly, so no quotation marks are used.

lessons.title: Quotations Inside Quotations
lessons.mainIdea: In American usage, single quotation marks show a quotation inside another quotation, and every quoted word must be exactly what the source said.
reading: Sometimes a speaker quotes someone else. "My mother always told me, 'Finish what you start,'" Dev said. The outer speech uses double quotation marks; the quotation inside it uses *single quotation marks*. Notice the ending: the single closing mark, then the comma, then the double closing mark, all together. It looks crowded, but each mark closes something that was opened. This is American practice. British books often reverse it, single outside and double inside. That is why a novel from London looks different from one printed in Chicago.

The same rule holds in an essay when you quote a text that itself contains a quotation. A passage from a story might read: The old man said, "Nobody ever leaves this town." If you quote that whole passage, the old man's words shift to single marks: The narrator reports that the old man said, 'Nobody ever leaves this town.' Any quotation marks that were in the original become single marks inside your double ones. If you quote only the old man's words directly, they go back in ordinary double marks, because now they are the outer quotation.

One rule stands over all the others: what is inside quotation marks must be exactly what the source said, letter for letter. You may not fix a speaker's grammar, cut a word silently, or change a tense to fit your sentence. If the quote does not fit, quote less of it or rebuild your sentence around it. Titles of short works, such as poems, songs and articles, take double quotation marks ("The Raven"). Titles of long works, such as books and films, are italicized. Quotation marks are a promise, and readers trust the promise.

words.d: the marks ' ' used in American style for a quotation inside another quotation
a quotation that appears inside a larger quotation
quoted words that match the source letter for letter, with nothing changed

look.title: Marks Inside Marks
look.text: A reporter writes: The coach told us, "When I asked the team what went wrong, one player said, 'We stopped listening to each other,' and that was the truest thing anyone said all season." Count the quotation marks and match each opening mark to its closing mark.
look.prompt: Who is speaking in the outer quotation and who in the inner one? If the reporter wanted to quote only the player, how would the marks change?

check.q: In American style, what marks go around a quotation inside a quotation?
choices: Double quotation marks
Single quotation marks
Parentheses
Italics
check.why: The outer quotation takes double marks; the one nested inside takes single marks.

check.q: A speaker said 'we was late.' What may you do when quoting it?
choices: Change it to we were late
Leave out the words silently
Quote it exactly as said, or quote less of it
Put the whole thing in italics
check.why: Quotation marks promise exact words. If the words do not fit, quote fewer of them or rebuild the sentence.

check.q: Which title is punctuated correctly according to the lesson?
choices: the poem The Raven, in italics
the poem 'The Raven,' in single quotation marks
the novel "Moby-Dick," in double quotation marks
the poem "The Raven," in double quotation marks
check.why: Short works such as poems take double quotation marks; long works such as novels are italicized.

lessons.title: Ellipses and Brackets
lessons.mainIdea: An ellipsis shows where you left words out of a quotation, and brackets show where you added or changed a word; both keep the reader honest.
reading: A source is long and you need one sentence of it. Cut words, but show the cut. An *ellipsis* is three spaced periods ( . . . ) that mark where words were removed from a quotation. Original: The bridge, which had stood for ninety years without a single repair, finally closed in March. Quoted: The bridge . . . finally closed in March. The reader knows something is missing and can go look. Never use an ellipsis to remove words that change the meaning. Cutting not from She did not agree and quoting She . . . agreed is not quoting; it is lying.

*Brackets*, the square marks [ ], show a word you added or changed inside a quotation. Original: He said it was the best game of his life. Quoted: He said it was "the best game of [his] life" needs no bracket, since his is in the original. But if the original said the best game of my life and your sentence needs his, write "the best game of [his] life." Brackets also explain a word the reader could not otherwise understand: "She [the principal] refused to comment." And the Latin word sic in brackets, [sic], marks an error that was in the original so the reader does not blame you: "We was [sic] ready."

Two habits finish the job. Do not put an ellipsis at the start of a quotation to show that words came before; readers assume that. And if you cut across the end of a sentence, keep the sentence's period plus the three dots, making four. In MLA style, an ellipsis is written as three periods with spaces between and around them; a keyboard's single ellipsis character is accepted by many teachers, but check. Ellipses and brackets look fussy, but they exist for one reason: to let you shape a quotation to fit your sentence while telling the reader exactly what you did.

words.d: three spaced periods that show where words were left out of a quotation
the square marks [ ] that show a word added or changed inside a quotation
a Latin word placed in brackets to show that an error was in the original

look.title: Frederick Douglass on Learning to Read
look.text: Douglass wrote that once he had learned the alphabet, his master forbade any further lessons. The prohibition, he said, taught him something the lessons had not: that reading was the path out of slavery, and he resolved to learn at any cost.
look.cite: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: This look paraphrases Douglass instead of quoting him. Why is a paraphrase never put in quotation marks, and what would you need before you could quote him with an ellipsis?

check.q: What does an ellipsis in a quotation tell the reader?
choices: That words were left out at that point
That the speaker paused
That the quotation is from a poem
That the writer added a word
check.why: In a quotation the three spaced periods mark a cut, so the reader knows the words are not continuous.

check.q: When should you use brackets inside a quotation?
choices: To show a pause
To show a word you added or changed
To mark the title of a short work
To show the quotation is from a secondary source
check.why: Brackets mark your own words inside someone else's, including a replaced pronoun, an explanation or [sic].

check.q: Why is quoting 'She . . . agreed' from 'She did not agree' dishonest?
choices: Because the ellipsis has the wrong number of periods
Because ellipses cannot be used mid-sentence
Because the cut reverses the source's meaning
Because brackets were required instead
check.why: An ellipsis may shorten a quotation but never change what the source actually said.

lessons.title: Capitalization and Titles
lessons.mainIdea: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, proper nouns and the main words of titles, and know that italics and quotation marks tell readers what kind of title it is.
reading: Capital letters mark starts and names. Every sentence starts with one. So does every *proper noun*, the name of a particular person, place or thing: Lake Michigan, the Eisenhower Expressway, Ms. Duarte, the Chicago Bears, Illinois. The common noun stays lowercase: a lake, a highway, a teacher, a team, a state. The trouble comes with words that can be either. Capitalize mom, dad, coach and professor when they stand in for a name (I asked Mom; Thanks, Coach) but not after my, the or a (I asked my mom; the coach). Capitalize a title right before a name (Governor Pritzker) but not on its own (the governor).

Seasons are lowercase (fall, winter), but days, months and holidays are capitalized (Tuesday, October, Thanksgiving). Directions are lowercase (drive north), but regions are capitalized (the South Side, the Midwest). Languages, nationalities and religions are capitalized (Spanish, Polish, Muslim). School subjects are lowercase (history, biology) unless they are languages or specific course titles (English, Biology 101). The rule under all of these: is this the name of one particular thing, or a general word? Names get capitals.

*Title case* means capitalizing the first and last words of a title and every main word between, while leaving small words lowercase: articles (a, an, the), short prepositions (of, in, to) and joining words (and, but, or). The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. A Raisin in the Sun. Then show what kind of work it is. Long works that stand on their own are italicized: books, plays, films, albums, newspapers, TV series. Short works that live inside something bigger take quotation marks: poems, short stories, articles, songs, single episodes. When you handwrite, underlining stands in for italics.

words.d: the name of a particular person, place or thing, always capitalized
capitalizing the first, last and main words of a title, with small words lowercase
slanted type used for titles of long, standalone works such as books and films

look.title: Capitals in a Title, Counted
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from the title The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
look.prompt: Which word is lowercase and why? Would it stay lowercase if the title were Of Mice and Men? Explain the rule for the first word.

check.q: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
choices: I asked Mom if the Coach had called.
I asked my Mom if the coach had called.
I asked my mom if coach had called.
I asked Mom if the coach had called.
check.why: Mom stands in for a name, so it is capitalized; the coach follows the, so it stays lowercase.

check.q: How is the title of a poem shown in an essay?
choices: In quotation marks, because a poem is a short work
In italics, because all titles are italicized
In all capital letters
Underlined and in quotation marks
check.why: Short works such as poems, songs and articles take quotation marks; long works take italics.

check.q: Which words stay lowercase in title case?
choices: Nouns and verbs
Short articles, prepositions and joining words in the middle of the title
The first and last words
Every word after the first
check.why: Words like a, of, in and and stay lowercase unless they begin or end the title.

lessons.title: Spelling in the Age of Autocorrect
lessons.mainIdea: Autocorrect fixes typos but not wrong words, so a writer still has to know the words that sound alike and proofread with human eyes.
reading: Autocorrect and spell-check catch words that are not words. They do not catch words that are real but wrong. Their, there and they're are all in the dictionary, so a phone will happily let you write Their going to be late. So will its and it's, your and you're, then and than, affect and effect, lose and loose, to, too and two. These *homophones*, words that sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning, cause most of the spelling errors readers actually notice. No software reads for meaning the way a reader does. That job is still yours.

Learn the handful of pairs that trip you, and give each one a test. It's is always it is or it has; if you cannot swap in it is, use its. You're is you are. They're is they are; there points to a place or starts a sentence; their shows ownership. Than compares; then tells when. Affect is usually the verb (the news affected her), effect usually the noun (the effect was clear). Lose is what happens to your keys; loose is what a shoelace gets. Ten minutes with these pairs saves years of small embarrassments.

Autocorrect brings its own errors, too: it changes an unusual name to a common word, swaps a slang word for a wrong formal one, or turns a correct word into a different one because you hit a key next to it. So *proofread*, which means reading a finished draft only for surface errors. Read it slowly, in a different font or on paper if you can, and read each word as it is, not as you meant it. Keep a personal list of your own repeat offenders. When you are truly stuck on a word, use the dictionary, not a guess and not the first suggestion your phone offers.

words.d: words that sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things, such as their and there
read a finished draft slowly, only to catch surface errors in spelling, punctuation and typing
software that changes what you type to what it guesses you meant

look.title: Every Word Is Real
look.text: A text message: Your going to loose you're mind when you here who's coming, its the hole team and there bringing they're trophy. Every single word in that message passes spell-check.
look.prompt: Find all eight wrong words and write the corrected message. Which pair do you personally mix up most often, and what test would catch it?

check.q: Why does spell-check miss errors like 'their going'?
choices: Because their is too short to check
Because spell-check only checks nouns
Because their is a real word; the software does not read for meaning
Because spell-check ignores the first word of a sentence
check.why: Spell-check compares words to a dictionary; both their and there are in it.

check.q: Which sentence uses its and it's correctly?
choices: The dog lost it's collar, and its a shame.
The dog lost its collar, and its a shame.
The dog lost it's collar, and it's a shame.
The dog lost its collar, and it's a shame.
check.why: Its shows ownership; it's means it is. Swap in it is to test each one.

check.q: What does proofreading mean, according to the lesson?
choices: Reading a finished draft slowly for surface errors
Rewriting the ideas of a draft
Running spell-check one more time
Having a friend summarize your draft
check.why: Proofreading is the last, slow reading for spelling, punctuation and typing mistakes.

lessons.title: MLA Format and Citations
lessons.mainIdea: MLA style tells a reader where your evidence came from through short in-text citations and a matching Works Cited list.
reading: When you use another writer's words or ideas, readers need to be able to find them. *MLA style*, the set of rules published by the Modern Language Association, is the one most English classes use. It has two parts that work together. The *in-text citation* is a short note in parentheses at the end of the sentence, usually the author's last name and the page number: Douglass describes learning to read in secret (Douglass 40). If you have already named the author in the sentence, give only the page: Douglass describes learning to read in secret (40). The period goes after the parentheses.

The second part is the *Works Cited* page, a list at the end of the paper, alphabetized by the authors' last names, giving the full information for every source you cited in the text. A basic book entry looks like this: Douglass, Frederick. Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave. Publisher, year. The book title is italicized. An article or web page puts its own title in quotation marks, followed by the italicized name of the website or magazine, the date, and the address. Every in-text citation must match one entry on this page, and every entry must be cited somewhere in the text.

MLA also sets the look of the paper: double spacing throughout, one-inch margins, a readable 12-point font, your last name and the page number in the top right corner of every page, and a four-line heading in the top left (your name, teacher, course, date) followed by a centered title. None of this is decoration. A format everyone shares lets the reader stop noticing the format and pay attention to the argument. When in doubt about a source type, consult the current MLA Handbook or your school library's guide rather than copying a citation you found online.

words.d: the rules for format and citation published by the Modern Language Association, used in most English classes
a short note in parentheses, usually author and page, showing where a quote or idea came from
the alphabetized list at the end of an MLA paper giving full information for every source cited

look.title: Match the Two Parts
look.text: A paper's Works Cited list has three entries: one for Frederick Douglass, one for Kate Chopin, one for a newspaper article with no author. In the text, the writer cites (Douglass 40), (Chopin 12) and (Twain 88). The paper also quotes the newspaper article but never cites it.
look.prompt: What are the two mismatches between the text and the Works Cited list? How should the newspaper article be cited in the text when there is no author?

check.q: What goes in an MLA in-text citation when the author is not named in the sentence?
choices: The title of the book and the year
The author's last name and the page number
The publisher and the year
The author's full name and the title
check.why: MLA in-text citations are short: last name and page, in parentheses before the period.

check.q: What is the relationship between in-text citations and the Works Cited page?
choices: The Works Cited page lists only sources you did not quote
In-text citations replace the Works Cited page
Every in-text citation matches one full entry on the Works Cited page
The Works Cited page lists every source you read, cited or not
check.why: The short citation in the text points the reader to the full entry at the end; the two lists must match.

check.q: Why does MLA fix details like margins, spacing and the header?
choices: To make papers longer
To show the teacher that the student followed rules
To make the paper look decorated
So a shared format lets readers focus on the argument instead of the layout
check.why: A common format becomes invisible, so attention goes to the writing.

review.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: Because it rained; the game was canceled.
It rained; the game was canceled.
It rained; and the game was canceled.
It rained; canceling the game.
review.why: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and It rained and the game was canceled are both complete.

review.q: What must be true of the words before a colon?
choices: They must be a list
They must end with a verb
They must form a complete sentence
They must be fewer than ten words
review.why: A colon follows a complete statement and points to what comes next.

review.q: 'My cousin, who plays drums, is visiting.' What do the commas tell you?
choices: The writer has several cousins
The clause identifies which cousin
The sentence is a comma splice
The writer has one cousin, and the drumming is extra information
review.why: Commas make the clause nonrestrictive: extra detail about a cousin already identified.

choices: a well known singer
a highly skilled singer
a singer who is well known
a very famous singer
review.why: Well-known is a compound modifier before a noun. No hyphen after -ly adverbs or after the noun.

review.q: Where do commas and periods go with quotation marks in American style?
choices: Outside the closing mark
Inside the closing mark
Inside only if the quotation is a full sentence
Either place, as the writer prefers
review.why: American practice always puts commas and periods inside the closing quotation mark.

review.q: What does [sic] inside a quotation mean?
choices: The writer added a word
Words were left out here
The error was in the original source
The quotation is translated
review.why: Sic tells the reader the mistake belongs to the source, not the writer quoting it.

review.q: Which title is formatted correctly for a novel?
choices: "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" in quotation marks
the adventures of huckleberry finn in lowercase
'The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn' in single marks
The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in italics
review.why: A novel is a long, standalone work, so its title is italicized and written in title case.

review.q: Why must a writer still proofread after running spell-check?
choices: Because spell-check cannot tell a real word used wrongly from the right word
Because spell-check only works on paper
Because spell-check cannot find misspelled words
Because MLA forbids spell-check
review.why: Homophones and autocorrect swaps are real words in the wrong place; only a reader catches them.
